records.answer: The LLM+P approach relies on an external classical planner for long-horizon planning [1, 2]. This approach uses the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) as an intermediate interface to describe the planning problem [1].
Short-Term Memory (STM) is believed to have the capacity of about 7 items [1]. It lasts for 20-30 seconds [1].

ANNOY uses random projection trees as its core data structure [1]. These are binary trees where each non-leaf node represents a hyperplane that splits the input space in half, and each leaf stores a single data point [1].

The main innovation of ScaNN is anisotropic vector quantization [2]. This method quantizes a data point $x_i$ to $\tilde{x}_i$ such that the inner product $\langle q, x_i \rangle$ is as similar as possible to the original distance of $\angle q, \tilde{x}_i$, rather than selecting the closest quantization centroid points [2].
API-Bank contains 53 commonly used API tools [1, 2]. It also includes 264 annotated dialogues [1, 2].
ChemCrow is augmented with 13 expert-designed tools [2].
In the Generative Agents Simulation, there are 25 virtual characters, each controlled by an LLM-powered agent [1].
The generative agents retrieval model uses relevance, recency, and importance to surface context to inform the agent's behavior [1].
Up to three reflections are added into the agent's working memory to be used as context for querying the LLM [1].
Four out of eleven requests were accepted to obtain a synthesis solution when the agent was asked to synthesize known chemical weapon agents [1].

The HuggingGPT system comprises four stages [1]. These stages are: (1) Task planning, where the LLM acts as the brain and parses user requests into multiple tasks; (2) Task process description and analysis/model inference results presentation to the user in the first person, which requires telling the user the complete file path if inference results contain one; (3) (This stage is not explicitly named but is implied between the first two stages); and (4) Response generation, where the LLM receives execution results and provides summarized results to users [1, 2].

HNSW builds hierarchical layers of small-world graphs, with the bottom layers containing the actual data points [2]. When searching, HNSW begins at a random node in the top layer and navigates toward the target [1]. This process involves moving down through layers, where moves in the upper layers can cover a large distance in the data space, and moves in the lower layers refine the search quality [1].

Zhao et al. (2021) proposed that several biases contribute to the high variance in few-shot classification when using LLMs [1]. These biases include:
*   Majority label bias, which occurs if the distribution of labels among the examples is unbalanced [1].
*   Recency bias, which is the tendency for the model to repeat the label at the end [1].
*   Common token bias, indicating that LLMs tend to produce common tokens more often than rare tokens [1].

Self-consistency sampling involves sampling multiple outputs with a temperature greater than 0 and then selecting the best one among these candidates [2]. A general method for selecting the best candidate is to use a majority vote [2].

The STaR method involves asking the LLM to generate reasoning chains and then only keeping those chains that lead to correct answers [2]. After this, the model can be fine-tuned using the generated rationales, and this process can be repeated until convergence [2].
When separating reasoning steps, the newline $\text{\n}$ symbol is better than using "step i, period ." or a semicolon ";" [1].

The augment-prune-select process for automatically constructing chain-of-thought prompts involves three steps [1]:
1. **Augment**: Generating multiple pseudo-chains of thought using few-shot or zero-shot CoT prompts given a question [1].
2. **Prune**: Filtering the pseudo chains based on whether their generated answers match the ground truths [1].
3. **Select**: Applying a variance-reduced policy gradient strategy to learn the probability distribution over the selected examples, while also considering the probability distribution over examples as the policy and the validation set accuracy as the reward [1].

Paragraphs were ranked using TF-IDF based cosine similarity between the evidence paragraphs and the query [1]. Lazaridou et al. (2022) studied using Google Search for document retrieval to augment LLMs [1, 3]. After extracting clean text from 20 URLs returned by Google, the resulting documents were split into paragraphs of 6 sentences, denoted as $\{p\}$ [1]. Only the most relevant paragraph was used in the prompt to generate an answer [1].

APE (Automatic Prompt Engineer) searches over a pool of model-generated instruction candidates [1]. It then filters this candidate set using a chosen score function to select the best candidate, which is the one with the highest score [1].

Self-Ask is a method that repeatedly prompts the model to ask follow-up questions to construct the thought process iteratively [1]. Follow-up questions can be answered using search engine results [1].
GBDA ("Gradient-based Distributional Attack") utilizes the Gumbel-Softmax approximation trick to make adversarial loss optimization differentiable [1].

Universal Adversarial Triggers (UATs) are considered universal because they are input-agnostic [1]. Furthermore, they can transfer between models that have different embeddings, tokenization, and architecture [1].

White-box attacks assume attackers have full access to the model weights, architecture, and training pipeline, allowing them to obtain gradient signals [1]. In the white-box setting, attackers have full access to the model parameters and architecture, enabling them to use gradient descent to programmatically learn effective attacks [3]. Black-box attacks, conversely, assume attackers only have access to an API-like service where they provide input $\mathbf{x}$ and receive a sample $\mathbf{y}$ without knowing further model details [1].
The Python framework TextAttack (Morris et al. 2020) implemented many word and token manipulation attack methods to create adversarial examples for NLP models [1].

TextFooler identifies the most important and vulnerable words that most alter the model's prediction [3]. It replaces these words with top synonyms based on word embedding cosine similarity [1]. Furthermore, TextFooler filters the replacement words by ensuring they maintain the same Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging and that the sentence-level similarity remains above a certain threshold [1].
EDA defines a set of simple and more general operations to augment text [1]. These operations include synonym replacement, random insertion, random swap, or random deletion [1].

HotFlip treats text operations as inputs in the vector space [2]. It measures the derivative of the loss with regard to these vectors [2]. The input vector is assumed to be a matrix of character-level one-hot encodings, $\mathbf{x} \in {0, 1}^{m \times n \times V}$ [2]. The process involves constructing a new vector $\mathbf{x}_{ij, a\to b}$ by changing a character from $a \to b$ [2].

Gradient based attacks only function in the white-box setting [2]. In the white-box setting, attackers have full access to the model parameters and architecture [2]. Gradient based attacks rely on gradient signals to learn an effective attack [4].

Attacks on text data are considered much more challenging than those on images because text operates in a discrete space [1]. In contrast, adversarial attacks on images operate in a continuous, high-dimensional space [1].
